derivation.title: Rigorous derivation
derivation.lead: From the ready-made material we will need only two bricks: the first law of thermodynamics and the equation of state pV = nRT. There will be no new postulates in the derivation, but there will be one assumption that we will name out loud and then test for strength.

steps.text: Let's start with the fact that the question 'what is the heat capacity of a gas' is posed incompletely. Heat capacity is the ratio of the heat received to the increase in temperature, but heat is not a function of state: it depends on the path by which the gas went from the initial point to the final point. Take the same portion of air and supply the same joules to it in two ways. In a rigid cylinder, the thermometer will go noticeably further than under a free piston—and these are not different substances, but different processes. Hence the two numbers in the reference book: 718 and 1005 joules per kilogram per degree, differing by exactly 1.40 times.
steps.latex: C \equiv \frac{\delta Q}{dT} \;\text{depends on path}; \qquad c_V^{\text{air}} = 718, \quad c_p^{\text{air}} = 1005 \ \frac{\text{J}}{\text{kg}\cdot\text{K}}
steps.figCaption: One gas, one portion of heat, two vessels: in a rigid cylinder the temperature rises more than under a free piston

steps.text: Let's fix the piston. Then the volume does not change, the gas does not move anything and does no work: in the first law, the second term vanishes, and all the supplied heat goes into internal energy. The definition of heat capacity at constant volume is obtained immediately, and this is precisely a definition, not a consequence. Note the index V on the partial derivative: it is a load-bearing structure here, not a decoration—about energy, they ask how it grows with temperature at constant volume, and another question would give another answer.
steps.latex: \delta Q = dU + p\,dV, \qquad dV = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; \delta Q = dU \;\Longrightarrow\; C_V \equiv \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial T}\right)_V
steps.figCaption: Piston on a stop: the gas does not move anything, and all the heat remains inside—in the speed of molecules

steps.text: Now let's release the piston and put a constant load on it so that the pressure remains unchanged. To the previous account is added the work of expansion. Let's calculate it for a mole of ideal gas: from pV = RT at constant p it follows that the product of p and the increase in volume equals R multiplied by the increase in temperature. This is the main surprise of the derivation—the surcharge per degree is R joules per mole and does not depend on pressure, volume, or whether we have helium or carbon dioxide. Under normal conditions, a mole occupies 24 liters, and for one degree it pushes the atmosphere apart by about 82 cubic centimeters.
steps.latex: p\,\Delta V = R\,\Delta T \quad (p = \text{const}), \qquad \delta Q_p = dU + p\,dV
steps.figCaption: Free piston with a load: the gas heats up and simultaneously lifts the atmosphere, and the price for this is exactly R per mole and per degree

steps.text: Subtract one from the other. The increase in internal energy is the same in both cases—and here lies the assumption without which the whole derivation is incorrect: the internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature, not on volume. Joule tested this in 1845: he released compressed gas into an evacuated vessel, so the gas did no work against anything, and the temperature did not change. So spreading molecules 'for free'—in the absence of forces between them—costs no energy. For the van der Waals gas from the first paragraph of this topic, the assumption is already incorrect; there molecules attract, and pulling them apart requires energy expenditure.
steps.latex: C_p = \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial T}\right)_p + R = C_V + R \;\Longrightarrow\; \boxed{\,C_p - C_V = R\,} \quad (\text{Mayer, 1842})
steps.figCaption: Two measured numbers and one difference: 29.10 minus 20.79 gives 8.31—the universal gas constant

steps.text: Mayer's relation gives the difference, but not the heat capacities themselves. The value of C_V has to be taken from counting: how many independent ways a molecule has to store energy. The equipartition theorem answers that for each such way there is on average half kT, and then the molar heat capacity equals i halves R. Let's check on the simplest gas. For monatomic helium, the molecule is a point; it can only move in three directions, so i = 3 and C_V should equal 12.47 J/(mol·K), and C_p—20.79. The reference book gives 12.5 and 20.79. Coincidence to the third significant digit, and there were no fitting parameters in the calculation.
steps.latex: \bar\varepsilon = \frac{i}{2}k_BT \;\Longrightarrow\; U = \frac{i}{2}RT, \quad C_V = \frac{i}{2}R; \qquad i = 3:\; C_V = 12{,}47,\; C_p = 20{,}79\ \frac{\text{J}}{\text{mol}\cdot\text{K}}
steps.figCaption: Three directions of motion—three degrees of freedom: the formula gives 12.47, helium shows 12.5

steps.text: We move to a diatomic molecule—and the count breaks. A dumbbell has three translational degrees, two rotational (around the axis of the dumbbell there is nothing to rotate) and two vibrational, because vibration along the bond stores energy twice: in speed and in stretching the spring. Total seven, so C_V should be 29.1. The measured heat capacity of nitrogen at room temperature is 20.8, that is, exactly five halves R. Two degrees of freedom simply do not respond. The explanation is not in the rigidity of the bond, but in the fact that energy is given out in portions: the vibrational step of nitrogen costs 3390 kelvins, the thermal trifle of 300 kelvins does not reach it, and the vibration is silent (the population of the first step is 1.2·10⁻⁵—the calculation is analyzed in the paragraph on the Boltzmann factor). The rotational step, on the contrary, costs only 2.9 kelvins and is wide open. Here the quantum sticks out of classical thermodynamics: the numbers are integers, but which ones—is decided not by the geometry of the molecule, but by temperature.
steps.latex: i_{\text{class}} = 3 + 2 + 2 = 7 \;\Rightarrow\; C_V = 29{,}1; \qquad \text{experiment: } C_V(\mathrm{N_2}) = 20{,}8 = \tfrac{5}{2}R; \qquad \theta_{\text{rot}} = 2{,}9\,\text{K} \ll T \ll \theta_{\text{vib}} = 3390\,\text{K}
steps.figCaption: Rotational steps are smaller than the thermal quantum and work; the vibrational one is eleven times more expensive than kT and is silent

steps.text: Since we now know how to calculate C_V, and we know the difference, we will also calculate the ratio. It turns out to be a pure fraction of an integer: γ = (i + 2)/i. This is the most practical quantity of the entire paragraph, and here's why. Heat capacity is difficult to measure: you need a calorimeter, you need to know the mass of the gas, you need to account for the heat capacity of the vessel itself and losses to the environment. And γ is dimensionless—it requires neither units of heat nor units of mass. Three possible values stand far apart: 1.67 for monatomic, 1.40 for diatomic, 1.29 for a molecule with unfrozen vibration. They just need to be distinguished, and this is already a task for any experiment where γ enters the answer.
steps.latex: \gamma = \frac{C_p}{C_V} = \frac{C_V + R}{C_V} = 1 + \frac{2}{i} = \frac{i+2}{i}: \qquad \tfrac{5}{3} = 1{,}67, \quad \tfrac{7}{5} = 1{,}40, \quad \tfrac{9}{7} = 1{,}29
steps.figCaption: Three values of γ on one scale: the fewer working degrees of freedom a molecule has, the larger γ is

steps.text: Such an experiment exists, and it does not even require a laboratory: sound. In a sound wave, compressions and rarefactions alternate thousands of times per second, heat does not have time to flow between neighboring regions, and the process goes along an adiabat—and γ enters it as an exponent (the adiabatic equation itself is derived in the topic on engines; we take it ready-made). Hence c = √(γp/ρ), that is, c = √(γRT/M). Newton in the 'Principia' considered compressions isothermal, which is equivalent to γ = 1, and got 290 m/s against the measured 343—a miss of fifteen percent that lasted more than a century until Laplace in 1816 put the adiabatic exponent back in place. Today the formula is read in the reverse direction: 343 m/s for air give γ = 1.40 and i = 5, helium's 1007 m/s give i = 3, and 267 m/s for carbon dioxide give i ≈ 6.9, because for a linear triatomic molecule the deformation vibration costs only 960 kelvins and at room temperature is almost half unfrozen. A stopwatch measured the number of degrees of freedom.
steps.latex: c = \sqrt{\frac{\gamma p}{\rho}} = \sqrt{\frac{\gamma R T}{M}} \;\Longrightarrow\; \gamma = \frac{c^{2}M}{RT}, \quad i = \frac{2}{\gamma - 1}; \qquad \mathrm{He}\ 1007, \;\text{air}\ 343, \;\mathrm{CO_2}\ 267\ \text{m/s}
steps.figCaption: Newton considered the wave isothermal and got 290 m/s; the adiabatic factor γ adds the missing fifteen percent

derivation.plateCap: On the left is the price of piston freedom: exactly R joules per mole and per degree, the same for any ideal gas. In the middle is the heat capacity itself, assembled from an integer number of working degrees of freedom. On the right is the dimensionless ratio that connects these two statements with a stopwatch and therefore is easiest to test in experiment.
derivation.note: Let's collect the assumptions, which are also the boundaries of the formulas. First: the gas is ideal, that is, U = U(T). As soon as the attraction of molecules ceases to be negligible—and in the first paragraph of this topic we folded it into the correction a/V²—the difference C_p − C_V ceases to equal R and begins to depend on volume; the general formula is given below, in the appendix. Second: the number i was considered integer and constant. In fact, this is not so, and the vibrational degree of freedom turns on not like a switch, but smoothly, smeared over several hundred degrees; integers are a good approximation only in the temperature window where all steps are certainly either much lower than kT or much higher. Third: air is not a gas, but a mixture, and all its 'diatomic' numbers are averaged over nitrogen, oxygen, and argon; a pure mixture of diatomic gases would give exactly 1.4000, argon raises the calculated value to 1.4015, and the slightly opened vibration of oxygen at room temperature (its $\theta = 2270$ K) pulls back to the reference 1.400—three decimal places here are not a decoration, but the result of opposing effects. Fourth: the equipartition theorem is a classical theorem, and it was derived for a system where energy can take any values; where this is not true, it does not 'slightly err' but gives a qualitatively wrong answer, and it was precisely on heat capacities that this was first discovered. Fifth: the formula for the speed of sound assumes that heat exchange does not have time at all and that all degrees of freedom have time to exchange energy with translational motion during one compression. The second condition for carbon dioxide is satisfied at the limit, and at high frequencies its γ changes before our eyes—this is also mentioned in the appendix.

math.title: The Math You'll Need Here
math.lead: Three places where it's easy to slip up on autopilot: the subscript on a partial derivative, the behavior of the exponential, and reading proportionality under a square root.

items.what: Partial derivative and what's in its subscript
items.why: The notation (∂U/∂T)_V reads: "we change the temperature, while keeping the volume constant." The subscript is not a marginal note, but half the problem statement: for a function of several variables, there is no "derivative with respect to T" — there is a derivative with respect to T along a chosen direction. For an ideal gas, both derivatives — at constant volume and at constant pressure — happen to coincide, because U doesn't depend on volume at all, and the whole Mayer's relation rests on that. Once the energy starts to depend on volume, the coincidence disappears: in general, C_p − C_V is assembled from three derivatives at once, and there you won't get R or any other universal constant. A useful skill: when you see a derivative without a subscript in thermodynamics, immediately ask what is held fixed — otherwise the expression is simply undefined.
items.latex: \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial T}\right)_V \neq \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial T}\right)_p \;\text{in general}; \qquad C_p - C_V = T\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial T}\right)_V\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_p

items.what: Exponential as a switch, not a slope
items.why: The fraction of molecules that reach a step of height θ is given by the factor exp(−θ/T), and its whole behavior is that it changes not gradually, but abruptly. At θ/T = 3, that's already five percent — the step is noticeably populated. At θ/T = 11.3, it's 1.2·10⁻⁵ — one molecule in eighty thousand is populated, and the contribution to heat capacity vanishes. Between these two cases, there's only a factor of nearly four in temperature, but the result differs by a factor of four thousand. Hence the integers in i: a degree of freedom almost always either fully works or fully stays silent, and the intermediate state occupies a narrow window. The exact form of the transition is the Einstein function, shown on the right; for small θ/T it tends to 1, i.e., to classical equipartition, and for large θ/T it falls off as an exponential. We won't dissect the Boltzmann factor itself here; it's derived in the topic on statistics.

items.what: Proportionality under the root: what affects what more strongly
items.why: In the speed of sound formula, under the square root there are two properties of the gas — the adiabatic index γ and the molar mass M. Both enter in the same form, but they differ greatly in magnitude. γ can only wander between 1.29 and 1.67, and its square root is between 1.14 and 1.29: a spread of only fifteen percent, no matter how you slice it. But the molar mass ranges from 2 g/mol for hydrogen to 44 for carbon dioxide and beyond, i.e., by tens of times, and its square root varies by factors. Practical conclusion: if the speed of sound in two gases differs by a factor of three, it's almost certainly due to mass, not molecular structure. Check with helium and air: mass gives a factor of 2.69, the index only 1.09, together 2.94, and the measured ratio 1007/343 equals 2.94.

example.title: Example with numbers
example.lead: Let's take a cubic meter of ordinary room air and heat it by ten degrees in two ways. Then, without touching the calorimeter at all, we'll extract the number of degrees of freedom from a single measured quantity—the speed of sound.
example.given: A cubic meter of air at 20 °C (293.15 K) and pressure 101,325 Pa. Molar mass of air M = 28.97 g/mol, C_V = 5/2·R, C_p = 7/2·R, R = 8.314 J/(mol·K). Heat by ΔT = 10 K first in a rigid container, then under a free piston. Second part: the measured speed of sound in the same air is c = 343 m/s—find γ and i from it.
example.law: Q = n·C·ΔT, where C equals C_V at constant volume and C_p = C_V + R at constant pressure; the number of moles is taken from pV = nRT. For the second part, γ = c²M/(RT) and i = 2/(γ − 1).

solution.text: How many moles fit in a cubic meter. This is the usual equation of state, and the number is useful to remember: at room conditions, a cubic meter of air contains just over forty moles, that is, about 1.2 kilograms.
Rigid container. No work is done, all heat goes into internal energy.
Free piston. Same plus work of expansion.

We'll compute the difference in two independent ways. First, via Mayer's relation. Second, honestly, through work: at constant pressure, the volume increases proportionally to absolute temperature; ten degrees from 293 give an increase of 3.4 percent in volume, that is, 34 liters, and pushing back the atmosphere takes p·ΔV. The numbers coincide to within rounding—and it couldn't be otherwise, since $p\,\Delta V = pV\,\Delta T/T = nR\,\Delta T$—and this is a check of the derivation.
solution.latex: n R \Delta T = 41{,}6 \cdot 8{,}314 \cdot 10 = 3459\ \text{J}; \qquad \Delta V = V\frac{\Delta T}{T} = \frac{10}{293{,}15} = 0{,}0341\ \text{m}^3, \quad p\,\Delta V = 101\,325 \cdot 0{,}0341 = 3456\ \text{J}

solution.text: Now the speed of sound. We substitute the measured 343 m/s and solve the formula for γ, and then for i. There are no thermal units in this calculation at all—only meters, seconds, kilograms, and kelvins.

example.answer: The rigid container requires 8.6 kJ, the free piston—12.1 kJ: heating at constant pressure costs forty percent more, and the entire difference, 3.46 kJ, went into expansion work. And the speed of sound 343 m/s gives γ = 1.398 and i = 5.02—those very five degrees of freedom obtained with a stopwatch and a ruler, without a single joule in the calculation.
example.check: Three checks. First—return to the numbers from the introduction: divide the obtained heats by the mass of air. The mass is 41.6 · 0.028 97 = 1.205 kg, so the specific heat capacities come out 8649/(1.205·10) = 718 and 12 106/(1.205·10) = 1005 joules per kilogram per degree. These are the two reference figures with which the paragraph began, and they were not substituted—they were obtained. Second check, common sense: 12 kJ is a kilowatt kettle working for twelve seconds. Warming a cubic meter of air by ten degrees indeed costs almost nothing, and all the difficulty of heating is not in the air itself, but in the fact that it leaks away and that walls have to be heated. Third, reverse: if in the calculation i had turned out to be about three, one should look for an error in the molar mass: for the same 343 m/s to give γ = 5/3, the air would have to weigh 34.5 g/mol instead of 29. And if it had come out seven, it would be worth checking the temperature: at 1000 K, γ of air drops to 1.34, and i there indeed approaches six.

constants.title: Constants of this section
constants.lead: Four numbers. The first is assigned by definition, the second lives in every ventilation calculation, the third is dimensionless and therefore measurable, the fourth explains why the second is not what classical theory promises.

items.name: Universal gas constant
items.why: Since 2019, it is not measured but calculated exactly: R = N_A·k_B, and both constants on the right-hand side are fixed by the definitions of units. In this section, R acquires a completely everyday meaning — it is the price of expansion: how many extra joules a mole of gas asks for each degree if it is allowed to push the atmosphere apart. In specific form for air, R/M = 287 J/(kg·K), which is exactly the difference 1005 − 718.
items.mnemo: "Eight and a third." The old form is also useful: in calories, R ≈ 1.987 ≈ 2 cal/(mol·K) — hence the rule that the difference in molar heat capacities is about two calories per degree.

items.name: Specific heat capacity of air at constant pressure
items.why: The working number for all ventilation and climate control: a cubic meter of air weighs 1.2 kg, so heating it by one degree costs about 1.2 kJ. Hence the quick estimate of supply unit power: if you supply 300 cubic meters per hour and heat by 25 degrees, that is 300·1.2·1005·25/3600 ≈ 2.5 kW. The pair c_V = 718 and c_p = 1005 differs by exactly 287, i.e., by R/M — Mayer's relation in specific form.
items.mnemo: "A thousand joules per kilogram per degree" — with an error of half a percent. The second figure, 718, is easily obtained by subtracting 287.

items.name: Heat capacity ratio (adiabatic index) of air
items.why: The only constant in this section that has no units — and that is why it is the easiest to measure: it is extracted from the speed of sound, from the pop of a cork, from the pressure change during rapid compression. The value 7/5 indicates that air molecules have five degrees of freedom. The number is not eternal: at 1000 K, vibrations of nitrogen and oxygen begin to unfreeze, and γ drops to 1.34 — so turbine and diesel calculations use a variable γ, not the textbook 1.4.
items.mnemo: Seven fifths — because i = 5. The whole table comes from one fraction (i + 2)/i: 5/3 for monatomic, 7/5 for diatomic, 9/7 — if a diatomic molecule also gets a vibration. Around 1.29 at room temperature, carbon dioxide also ends up, but for its own reason: its deformation vibration is partially unfrozen.

items.name: Characteristic vibrational temperature of the nitrogen molecule
items.why: The price of the first vibrational step of the N—N bond, expressed in degrees: kθ = ħω. At 300 K, the ratio θ/T is 11.3, the Boltzmann factor gives 1.2·10⁻⁵, and the vibrational degree of freedom drops out of the heat capacity — hence the five instead of seven. For comparison, the rotational step of the same nitrogen costs 2.9 K, i.e., it is open in any weather. A detailed calculation of occupancy is in the section on the Boltzmann factor.
items.mnemo: Three thousand four hundred degrees — that is almost the melting point of tungsten (3695 K). The vibrational quantum of nitrogen is so expensive that at such a temperature the most refractory metal is already almost flowing.

synthesis.title: How This Connects to the Rest of the Course
synthesis.lead: The number of degrees of freedom is the most portable result of this section: it appears in engines, in thermal conductivity, in statistics, and even in solids, where there are no gas molecules at all.

items.text: The exponent γ, obtained here from counting degrees of freedom, appears as the exponent in the adiabatic equation pV^γ = const, and through it, in the compression temperature and in efficiency. In the topic on engines, we took γ directly from the geometry of the molecule; now it is clear that geometry sets only the upper limit, while how many degrees of freedom actually work is decided by temperature. A diesel engine ignites fuel without a spark precisely because γ > 1: compression by a factor of twenty raises the air temperature by 20^0.4 ≈ 3.3 times, that is, from 300 to a thousand kelvins. If γ were equal to one (that is, if the molecule had infinitely many working degrees of freedom), compression would not heat at all, and heat engines as we know them would not exist.

The freezing out of vibrations, which makes i equal to five instead of seven, is purely the exponential exp(−θ/T) from the topic on statistics. There it is derived and calculated quantitatively: θ = 3390 K, the ratio is 11.3, the population is 1.2·10⁻⁵. Here we use the result as a ready-made rule: a degree of freedom works if its quantum is cheaper than kT. Heat capacity turned out to be the first place in physics where energy quantization manifested itself in a macroscopic measurement — thirty years before it was given a name.

In the formula for the thermal conductivity of a gas κ = ⅓·n·v̄·λ·c, the last factor is the heat capacity of a single molecule, c = (i/2)k_B, that is, the same counting of degrees of freedom, but per particle rather than per mole. Therefore, helium conducts heat better than nitrogen at equal concentration not because of its degrees of freedom, but despite them: it has fewer of them, and the factor c loses — but the light molecule flies faster and travels farther, and the gain in v̄ and λ more than compensates for this loss. There also appears the Prandtl number, which contains the ratio of C_p to C_V — another place where γ comes to the fore.

The same counting works in a crystal: an atom in a lattice has three directions of vibration, each storing energy twice, giving a total of six halves of kT, that is, C = 3R = 24.9 J/(mol·K) — the Dulong–Petit law. It holds for copper, silver, and lead, but fails for diamond, whose heat capacity at room temperature is only 6.1: the bonds in diamond are stiff, the vibrational quanta are expensive, and most of the degrees of freedom are frozen out in exactly the same way as the vibration of nitrogen. Einstein analyzed this case in 1907, Debye refined it in 1912, and the quanta of lattice vibrations have been called phonons ever since.

items.h: The First and Second Sections of This Topic
items.text: Mayer's relation is derived for an ideal gas. A real gas from the first section, with its corrections a and b, gives a different difference in heat capacities, and the closer to the critical point, the stronger the discrepancy: at the critical point itself, C_p goes to infinity, because there the gas expands at constant pressure without any resistance. The surface from the second section also has its own heat capacity, and this is why σ decreases with temperature — but that is another story.

curiosities.title: Fun: Test with your own hands
curiosities.lead: Both experiments below are heard with your ears, not seen with your eyes: γ enters the speed of sound, and therefore the pitch. The kitchen turns out to be a perfectly suitable acoustics laboratory.

items.h: The bottle's hum drops if you pour carbon dioxide into it
items.text: Take two identical empty bottles. Blow across the neck of the first one — you'll get a steady hum; remember its pitch (or record it on your phone and compare later with any tuner). Into the second, put a spoonful of baking soda, pour in a little vinegar, and once the foam settles, carefully 'pour' the gas from that bottle into a third, dry and empty one: carbon dioxide is one and a half times heavier than air and pours almost like water. Do not screw the cap on any bottle — the gas is released vigorously, and a closed bottle becomes a pressure vessel. Now blow across the neck of the third bottle. The tone is noticeably lower.
items.answer: A bottle with a neck is a Helmholtz resonator, and its frequency is directly proportional to the speed of sound in the gas inside. In pure carbon dioxide, c = 267 m/s versus 343 in air, a ratio of 0.78 — that's a drop of 435 cents, i.e., a bit more than a major third and less than a fourth. But you won't have pure gas in the bottle: pouring gives a mixture, about seventy percent carbon dioxide and thirty percent remaining air. Let's calculate honestly for such a mixture: molar mass 39.5 g/mol instead of 44, γ = 1.31 instead of 1.29, speed 285 m/s — and the drop comes out to about 320 cents, i.e., roughly a minor third, three semitones. That's exactly what you should expect by ear; if you hear more than four semitones, you were lucky with gas purity. Note that the tone changes doubly: both the molar mass increased and γ decreased, because a triatomic molecule has more degrees of freedom active. The same experiment with helium from a balloon gives the opposite effect and much stronger: in helium, sound travels 2.94 times faster, and the hum goes up by 1865 cents, i.e., about one and a half octaves.

items.h: The tone of hot cocoa creeps upward
items.text: Put a spoonful of cocoa or instant coffee into a mug, pour hot water over it, and stir vigorously. Now start tapping the bottom of the mug rhythmically with a spoon — once per second, without stopping, for about twenty seconds. The first taps give a dull low sound, and then the pitch creeps upward and over ten seconds rises by a third, and if you're lucky, almost an octave. No cooling occurs during this time, and the pitch changes not because of temperature.
items.answer: The culprit is air bubbles that you mixed in with the powder. The frequency at which the mug with liquid resonates is proportional to the speed of sound in that liquid, and the speed of sound is the square root of the ratio of elasticity to density. Bubbles add almost nothing to density — air is a thousand times lighter than water — but they catastrophically spoil elasticity: compressing water is hard, but a bubble compresses readily, and the elasticity of the mixture is set by it. Moreover, on sound frequencies the bubble compresses adiabatically, so its elasticity is γp — and here the adiabatic index from our paragraph comes straight into the kitchen. Order of magnitude: with a bubble fraction of one thousandth of the volume, the speed of sound in the mixture drops to about 365 m/s versus 1500 in pure water — a factor of four. Bubbles rise and dissolve, the fraction falls, the speed grows, the pitch creeps up. The effect is called the hot chocolate effect; Frank Crawford described it carefully in 1982, and it works with any powder that brings air with it.

items.h: A heater does not increase the energy of the air in a room
items.text: You turned on the heater, the temperature in the room rose from 18 to 24 degrees. By how much did the internal energy of the air in the room increase?
items.answer: By nothing. The room communicates with the outside — cracks, ventilation, gaps — so the pressure in it is constant and equal to atmospheric. Let's write the internal energy of the air in a room of volume V: U = n·C_V·T, and the number of moles itself equals pV/(RT). The temperature cancels, and we are left with U = (i/2)·p·V, where there is no temperature at all. For a room of 50 cubic meters, this is 2.5 · 10⁵ · 50 = 12.5 megajoules at any temperature. The heat given off by the heater went not into the air but outside — together with some of the molecules that left, making room for the expanded rest. So where does the coziness go? First, not only the air heats up, but also the walls, furniture, floor, and their heat capacity is orders of magnitude larger. Second, comfort is set not by the energy of the air but by its temperature: it determines both the heat loss from your skin and the rate of evaporation from it. The paradox perfectly shows that 'the amount of heat in a room' is not a physical quantity but a colloquial phrase.

items.h: Maxwell admitted the defeat of molecular theory
items.text: The equipartition theorem is a beautiful and general result: each degree of freedom gets half kT, with no exceptions. The trouble is that when counting from spectra, a diatomic molecule has clearly more than seven degrees of freedom (the internal motions of atoms alone give a whole forest), while the measured heat capacity stubbornly gave five. Maxwell in an 1875 lecture called this the most notable failure of molecular theory and did not hide the problem behind caveats. Kelvin later included the same story among the 'clouds' over 19th-century physics.
items.answer: The solution came from where it was least expected. In 1900, Planck introduced quanta while dealing with radiation, and in 1907 Einstein applied the same idea to the heat capacity of solids and obtained its decrease upon cooling — the very thing classical theory could not do. After that, it became clear for gases too: a degree of freedom is not 'present' or 'absent'; it is switched on if its quantum is cheaper than kT. The beauty of the story is that the quantum could have been noticed in heat capacity tables half a century before Planck, no spectroscopy required. It was lying there, in plain sight, in the difference between five and seven.

items.h: Diamond is colder than classical physics allows
items.text: The same counting of degrees of freedom in a solid gives the Dulong–Petit law: an atom in a lattice has three directions of vibration, each counted twice (motion and elasticity), totaling six halves of kT and a molar heat capacity of 3R = 24.9 J/(mol·K). It checks out beautifully: copper 24.4, silver 25.4, lead 26.4 — all around 25, regardless of what the metal is.
items.answer: Now diamond: 6.1 J/(mol·K) at room temperature, four times less than promised. The reason is exactly the same as for nitrogen with its five instead of seven. Carbon–carbon bonds in diamond are extremely stiff, the vibrational quanta are correspondingly expensive, the characteristic temperature is about 2000 kelvins, and at 300 K most vibrational degrees of freedom are frozen out. Heat the diamond to a thousand degrees — the heat capacity rises to the Dulong–Petit limit. The same mechanism, the same exponential, a different scale. Incidentally, it is the stiffness of bonds that makes diamond a record holder in thermal conductivity: phonons in it travel fast and far, although there are few of them.

blocks.h: Mayer's relation holds only for an ideal gas
blocks.text: In general, the difference in heat capacities is expressed through derivatives of the equation of state and is not equal to any universal constant. For an ideal gas, both derivatives are computed mentally and yield exactly R. For a van der Waals gas from the first section, a correction appears that grows with density and with approach to the critical temperature — near the critical point the denominator goes to zero, and the difference diverges to infinity. For condensed media, the formula also works, but the result turns out to be tiny: for water at 25 °C, the difference C_p − C_V is only 0.79 J/(mol·K) — ten times smaller than R, because water hardly expands when heated. Hence the practical rule: for liquids and solids, reference books list C_p and the difference is usually neglected, while for gases it must be taken into account.
blocks.latex: C_p - C_V = -T\frac{(\partial V/\partial T)_p^{2}}{(\partial V/\partial p)_T}; \qquad \text{vdW: } C_p - C_V = \frac{R}{1 - \dfrac{2a(V-b)^{2}}{RTV^{3}}}

blocks.h: Degrees of freedom are not switched on by a toggle
blocks.text: The integer i is a convenient idealization. In reality, each vibrational mode contributes a smooth function of temperature to the heat capacity, and the transition from "silent" to "active" is smeared over about an order of magnitude in T. Let us calculate this for nitrogen using the Einstein formula on the right: at 300 K, vibration adds only 0.0016·R to C_V, i.e., six hundredths of a percent; at 1000 K it is already 0.41·R (the heat capacity grows from 2.50·R to 2.91·R, i.e., by almost seventeen percent); at 3000 K — 0.90·R out of the unit promised by classical theory. There is no click; there is a smooth rise spanning thousands of degrees. Rotations are quantized too, but their steps are usually small; an exception is hydrogen, whose rotational θ is about 85 K: its C_V slides down from 5/2·R starting already around 200 K and by 60 kelvins reaches 3/2·R — a diatomic gas begins to behave like a monatomic one. With hydrogen it gets even more interesting: its ortho and para forms have different rotational ladders and interconvert very slowly, so the measured heat capacity depends on how long the sample has been kept cold.

blocks.h: The exponent γ has a frequency dependence
blocks.text: The formula c = √(γRT/M) silently assumes that during one compression all degrees of freedom manage to exchange energy with translational motion. For air this holds with a huge margin. But for carbon dioxide, the deformation vibration is excited slowly: the molecule needs thousands of collisions to absorb or release a vibrational quantum. At low frequencies, sound manages to "see" the full heat capacity and travels at 267 m/s. At high frequencies, the vibration does not have time to engage, the effective γ rises toward 1.40, and the speed increases to 278 m/s — by four percent. Between these regimes lies a region of strong absorption: the wave's energy leaks into vibrations and returns with a delay. This is why carbon dioxide dampens sound so effectively, and it is through this absorption that intramolecular relaxation rates are measured.

blocks.h: Air is a mixture, and it can be humid
blocks.text: All the "diatomic" numbers for air are the result of averaging over 78 percent nitrogen, 21 percent oxygen, and almost one percent monatomic argon. Argon slightly shifts the calculated γ upward from exactly 1.4000 to 1.4015, while oxygen's vibration pulls it back: its characteristic temperature is 2270 K; at 293 K, the Einstein function gives 0.026 per molecule — a tiny contribution, but enough to bring the calculation back to 1.4004. The reference value 1.400 turns out to be the result of two opposing effects, not a simple fraction 7/5. Humidity acts in the opposite direction and more strongly than it seems: a water molecule weighs 18 g/mol versus 29 for average air, so humid air is LIGHTER than dry air, and sound travels faster in it. Let us calculate the limiting case: at 30 °C and full humidity, water vapor in air is 4.2 percent by volume, the average molar mass drops from 28.97 to 28.5 g/mol, and this alone adds 0.8 percent to the speed. At the same time, γ drops from 1.400 to 1.397, because triatomic water has more active degrees of freedom, but this takes away only 0.13 percent — an effect six times weaker than the mass effect. The net result is about plus 0.7 percent; at 20 °C it is half that, 0.4 percent. For comparison, temperature does incomparably more: from 0 to 30 °C, the speed of sound rises from 331 to 349 m/s, i.e., by five percent.

memo.essence: Heat capacity is a property of a process, not a substance. At constant pressure, a gas, in addition to being heated, pushes the atmosphere apart, and the surcharge is exactly R per mole per degree: C_p − C_V = R. C_V itself is given by counting the active degrees of freedom, C_V = (i/2)R, and their number is determined not by the geometry of the molecule, but by temperature: a step works if its quantum is cheaper than kT. The ratio γ = (i+2)/i is dimensionless and therefore is measured by the speed of sound.

where: Ventilation and climate control: a cubic meter of air weighs 1.2 kg, and heating it by one degree costs about 1.2 kJ
Diesel: compression by twenty times raises the temperature by 20^0.4 ≈ 3.3 times — fuel ignites without a spark plug, all because γ > 1
Acoustics: the speed of sound depends on temperature and not on pressure, so in frost sound travels slower
Helium in the voice: the pitch does not 'rise' — the resonances of the larynx shift upward because in helium sound travels 2.9 times faster
Turbine and engine design: at high temperatures γ drops from 1.40 to 1.34, and the textbook 1.4 has to be replaced with a table
memo.watchOut: Three traps. First — saying 'heat capacity of air' without specifying what is fixed: the difference between 718 and 1005 is forty percent, and in ventilation calculations this is not a trifle. Second — considering i a geometric characteristic of the molecule: for the same nitrogen molecule, i equals five at room temperature and tends to seven at three thousand kelvins. Third — thinking that the speed of sound increases with pressure: the formula includes the ratio γp/ρ, and when a gas is compressed both grow, so the dependence remains only on temperature.

quiz.q: A mole of helium is heated by 1 K at constant pressure, spending 20.79 J. The same mole is heated by 1 K in a rigid container, spending 12.47 J. Where did the missing 8.3 J go in the first case?
options: They went into expansion work: the gas pushed the atmosphere, and the payment is R·ΔT
They went into heating the piston and cylinder walls themselves
They went into exciting rotations — at constant pressure, molecules start to rotate
Nowhere: 8.31 J is calorimeter error, the heat capacities are actually equal
quiz.why: At constant pressure, the volume of a mole grows with temperature: from pV = RT it follows that p·ΔV = R·ΔT, i.e., exactly 8.314 J per degree. This work is done against the atmosphere and does not remain in the gas. The answer about heating the piston and walls is wrong because the heat capacity of the container is not part of the molar heat capacity of the gas; it is subtracted by separate calibration. The answer about exciting rotations is doubly impossible: helium is monatomic, there is nothing to rotate, and the number of active degrees of freedom depends on temperature, not on whether the piston is free or not. The answer about calorimeter error contradicts arithmetic: 20.79/12.47 = 1.667 = 5/3, too precise a ratio for an error.
quiz.hint: Write the first law: the heat supplied goes into the increase in internal energy plus work. The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature, and the temperature increased equally in both experiments.

quiz.q: The speed of sound in helium is 1007 m/s, in air 343 — 2.94 times greater. Helium is monatomic (γ = 1.67) and light (M = 4 g/mol). What gives the main contribution to this factor of 2.94?
options: Molar mass: it gives a factor of 2.69, while γ gives only 1.09
The adiabatic index: γ for helium is almost twice as large, and that decides it
Both contributions are roughly equal: about 1.7 from mass and about 1.7 from γ
Neither: helium is lighter, so its molecules move faster, and mass and γ are not in the formula
quiz.why: In the formula c = √(γRT/M), both properties are under the root, but their ranges are incomparable. The ratio of molar masses is 28.97/4.00 = 7.24, its square root is 2.69. The ratio of adiabatic indices is 1.667/1.400 = 1.19, its root is 1.09. The product 2.69 · 1.09 = 2.94 — exactly the measured value. The answer 'the adiabatic index decides' is numerically wrong: γ for helium is only 19% larger than for air, not twice. The answer 'neither' correctly senses the physics (helium molecules are indeed faster), but that is exactly what is written in the formula as the factor 1/√M — there is no separate mechanism here. General rule: γ varies between 1.29 and 1.67, while molar mass varies by tens of times, so large differences in sound speed are almost always about mass.
quiz.hint: Calculate the two roots separately: the root of the ratio of γ and the root of the inverse ratio of molar masses. Which one is further from unity?

quiz.q: In your own words: for a diatomic nitrogen molecule, the classical count gives seven degrees of freedom, but the measured heat capacity corresponds to five. Why?
quiz.why: Because energy cannot be delivered in arbitrarily small portions. Three translational and two rotational degrees of freedom work: the rotational step of nitrogen costs 2.9 K, and the thermal energy at 300 K covers it with a huge margin. The two vibrational ones do not work: the vibrational step of the N—N bond costs 3390 K, i.e., eleven times more than kT at room temperature, and the Boltzmann factor gives a population of 1.2·10⁻⁵ — about one molecule in eighty thousand vibrates, and such a contribution to heat capacity is not measurable. Hence i = 3 + 2 + 0 = 5 and C_V = 5/2·R = 20.8 J/(mol·K). Importantly, the molecule is not 'rigid' — it is quite capable of vibrating, but at 300 K only a vanishing fraction does. Heat nitrogen to a thousand kelvins, and the heat capacity will creep up, and by three thousand it will approach the promised seven halves of R.
quiz.hint: Compare two quantities: the price of one quantum of nitrogen vibration (in degrees it is 3390 K) and the thermal small change available to a molecule at 300 K. Which is larger and by how much?

quiz.q: Argon is monatomic, its molar mass is 39.95 g/mol. Estimate the speed of sound in argon at 20 °C (293 K). Answer in meters per second. Use R = 8.31 J/(mol·K).
quiz.why: Monatomic gas — so i = 3 and γ = (3 + 2)/3 = 5/3 = 1.667. Substitute: c = √(γRT/M) = √(1.667 · 8.31 · 293 / 0.03995) = √(4058/0.03995) = √101600 ≈ 319 m/s. The reference value is 319 m/s. A quick estimate without a calculator: argon is 1.5 times heavier than air (39.95 vs 28.97, ratio 1.38, root 1.17), but γ is larger by 1.19 times (root 1.09), so c should be about 343 · 1.09/1.17 ≈ 320 m/s. A useful error check: 292 m/s means you took γ = 1.4 instead of 5/3, and ten meters per second means the molar mass stayed in grams.
quiz.hint: First determine γ: for a monatomic gas only three translational degrees of freedom work. Convert the molar mass to kilograms per mole, otherwise the answer will be off by a factor of thirty.

en.title: Heat Capacities C_V and C_p: Where Does the Heat Go
en.subtitle: Section 3 · Mayer's relation, degrees of freedom, and the speed of sound
intro: Open a reference book at the word 'air' and find the heat capacity. There will be two numbers: 718 and 1005 joules per kilogram per degree. They differ by forty percent, both are correct, and neither is a typo. The substance is the same, the temperature is the same, but there are two answers—because the question was not fully specified.

The difference arises from what we held fixed while heating. A gas in a rigid cylinder can only get hotter. A gas under a free piston heats up and, in passing, pushes the atmosphere apart, and that requires work, and someone has to pay for it—the same stove pays. Hence the second number. Remarkably, the surcharge is calculated exactly, in one line, and does not depend on what the gas is: this is Mayer's relation.

Next, we will ask where the value of C_V itself comes from, and we will obtain it by counting the directions in which a molecule can move. The count will give seven for a diatomic gas, but experiment stubbornly shows five, and at this point quantum mechanics pokes out of classical thermodynamics. And in the end, it turns out that the number of degrees of freedom can be measured with a stopwatch: the ratio γ = C_p/C_V is dimensionless and therefore reads directly from the speed of sound.
en.standNote: The stand for this topic draws van der Waals isotherms, and you should take one detail from it—the gray dashed hyperbola labeled 'ideal gas'. It is always drawn: it is the same gas, calculated using $pV = nRT$. Everything we derive below lives on it—the relation $C_p - C_V = R$ relies on the fact that internal energy depends only on temperature, and that is true where the gas is ideal. Set the reduced temperature to $T/T_c = 1.30$ and move the volume slider all the way to the right: the solid curve approaches the dashed line but does not merge with it—the lower panel, where $Z = pV/nRT$ is plotted, shows 0.91 instead of unity. Return the volume to $V/V_c = 1$, and $Z$ drops to 0.63. The stand simply does not reach the ideal gas, and that is honest: the room air from our example sits at $V/V_c$ around two hundred fifty, far beyond the right edge of the graph—there $Z$ is indeed unity. Now lower the temperature to 1.00 and look at the left half: the curves diverge, and with them the heat capacities diverge. At the critical point itself, the tangent to the isotherm becomes horizontal, meaning the gas expands at constant pressure with no resistance at all—and the difference $C_p - C_V$ turns not into $R$, but into infinity. Keep this picture in mind: it shows the boundary beyond which the neat formula of this section stops working.

formula.story: Mayer era médico de a bordo. En 1840 navegaba hacia Java y, al sangrar a los marineros, notó que la sangre venosa en los trópicos era más clara de lo normal — como si en un clima cálido el cuerpo quemara menos oxígeno. De ahí llegó a la idea de que el calor y el trabajo son lo mismo, solo que en diferentes monedas, y el tipo de cambio es constante. No tenía con qué calcular ese tipo de cambio: no tenía instrumentos. Tomó las capacidades caloríficas tabuladas del aire a presión constante y a volumen constante, restó una de la otra y declaró que la diferencia es exactamente el calor que se fue para expandir la atmósfera. La lógica es impecable, y la repetiremos a continuación palabra por palabra. El resultado fue casi un quince por ciento inferior al correcto — 3,58 julios por caloría en lugar de 4,18 — simplemente porque las capacidades caloríficas tabuladas de aquella época eran malas. La historia posterior no es alegre. El artículo de Mayer fue rechazado al principio, la prioridad se le dio a Joule, que midió el mismo tipo de cambio con experimentos cuidadosos, y el propio Mayer en 1850 se arrojó por una ventana y pasó varios años en un sanatorio. El reconocimiento llegó en los años sesenta, cuando Tyndall y Clausius devolvieron su trabajo a la circulación. La fórmula que dedujo a partir de dos números ajenos y un razonamiento sigue en los libros de texto hasta hoy.
